Gautrain 2.0 – Full Steam Ahead, or Financial Dead-End?

By: Layton Beard | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche we ask if the proposed Gautrain expansion will transform the province’s transport, or be a fast-track to spending billions on a single project

Unique Selling Point:
A comprehensive, easy-to-understand explanation of the current Gautrain costs, the proposed expansion plans, and what the people who are most affected have to say about it. Unlike other reports which have already been written on the proposed extensions, this story will unpack the contentious issue of the justification of the expansions, especially in the context of the current system which has already cost Gauteng taxpayers close to R23bn because of low ridership numbers.

Summary:
Hailed as an answer to Gauteng’s congestion problems – specifically on the N1 between Tshwane and Johannesburg - the Gautrain has failed to reach pre-launch ridership numbers or reduce congestion. While it is world class, clean, on time, and safe, the Gautrain is also expensive and out of reach of poorer commuters, it is aimed at people who are already mobile, and it is running at a massive loss, costing taxpayers billions of Rands through the PG annually. Gautrain expenditure is also diverting funds from other transport solutions in poorer communities, raising the question of where the GPG’s priorities lie in providing mobility solutions for all in the province. In this context, is an extension of the service (which will cost additional billions to construct and maintain) viable and necessary, and why does the Gauteng Premier, his government, and the GMA believe it is? Critically, the piece will also ask the question of why there is so much secrecy around the project, and why the GPG and the GMA have been more forthcoming with the public.

Further information:
Interviews with affected residents from Sharonlea and with the CEO of the Gautrain Management Agency - Tshepo Kgobe

Extra Budget Items:
None expected.

Press Release:


Gautrain 2.0
It was hailed as the answer to Gauteng’s traffic problems, but the Gautrain has failed to reach projected ridership… or reduce congestion. Instead, while it offers a clean, safe world-class service, the Gautrain remains out of reach for commuters who depend on public transport. And it’s running at a massive loss. But that hasn’t stopped management and provincial government pushing a multi-billion-rand extension of the service. Will the proposed expansion transform the province’s transport? Or is it no more than an expensive showpiece? Carte Blanche asks: full steam ahead, or financial dead end?
Producer: Layton Beard | Presenter: Govan Whittles


Script:


Gautrain 2.0 (Commission # 6873)
SCRIPT

(Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi) Madam Speaker … we are expanding Gautrain… Gauteng will invest 120 billion

(Panyaza Lesufi) Gauteng will invest 120 billion

(Govan) It’s a now familiar commitment from Gauteng Premier Panyaza Lesufi: the promise of a better public transport system. A godsend for some, a financial blunder and waste of taxpayer’s money for others. The Gautrain runs between Pretoria, Joburg, and OR Tambo International Airport. It cost around 30 billion rand to build, with government promising a mass transit solution for the province

(Govan) Unfortunately, these empty seats are a familiar sight on the Gautrain … that’s because it’s never achieved the ridership numbers it promised in 2010 when it launched. In fact, taxpayers have had to subsidise the shortfall to the tune of R23bn since 2013.

(Govan) Unknown to many, that 23 billion has come directly from the Gauteng Province’s Transport Budget – three billion in 2025 alone. That means that before a single cent is spent on infrastructure or other modes of public transport in the province – billions must first be paid to the private operating company as compensation for the low ridership numbers …In a country desperate for money to fund its many commitments, that’s a bitter pill. And yet, there are plans to expand the Gautrain service– with an initial estimated cost four times the cost of the original system.

(Govan) Tshepo Kgobe is the CEO of the Gautrain Management Agency – or GMA. He says that requirement – known as the patronage guarantee – won’t be written into new contracts

(Tshepo Kgobe) For me, looking back at it, I could always say that what do they call it, I am not happy about it because that is a contract I have to run now, it is what do they call it, it is a contract that, what do they call it, I’ve struggled to keep in check and make sure that it doesn’t what do they call it doesn’t run away with us over the period of time, but it is in today’s times, and what do they call it, it is in understanding projects like this that that is not a contract that we could ever, ever sign again.

(Govan) The original vision was to create a service more expensive than a taxi, but cheaper than a private car. But that’s put a regular ticket beyond the reach of many - raising the question: is it really a mobility solution for all? The Automobile Association hasn’t minced its words on that question: it’s labelled the Gautrain a railway of the elite – describing it as a system that is underused and overfunded. The AA says while the Gautrain may be a technical success it is priced beyond the reach of poorer communities, adding that a transit system that repairs and responds to the South African reality is needed. In other words, on a purely ethical basis, poor people are left in the lurch.

(Govan) And residents in parts of Joburg and Pretoria believe they are, too. But for different reasons. Places like Hazeldean, Irene, Sunninghill, Fourways, Boksburg, and Mamelodi will eventually be impacted by the extensions. Phase One of the planned expansion, though, cuts through the leafy suburb of Sharonlea. The estimated costs of the expansion includes paying the residents for properties that’ll have to make way for new tracks and stations.

(Govan) This one of the more established neighbourhoods in Joburg, and if you’ve bought a home here, there’s not much else you can do but take the payout. It seems like an incredibly unfair proposition to the residents of Sharonlea. They don’t have much choice.

(Govan) Nicolette Joubert is the Chairperson of the Sharonlea Action Group and has lived in her house for more than two decades …

(Nicolette Joubert) According to the line and the maps, the line is coming directly through this house.
(Govan) that’s the Gautrain line?
(Nicolette) That’s the Gautrain line … ja, so …
(Govan) how do you feel about that?
(Nicolette Joubert) Not good.

(Govan) Officially known as the Gautrain Rapid Rail Integrated Network extensions – the expansion of the Gautrain comes with more than just a massive price tag … for residents, the extension plans – literally – hit too close to home …

(Govan) Long-time Sharonlea resident JC Wouters is the Chairman of the Resident’s Forum.

(JC Wouters) The big problem is that we’ve got an established community – personally myself, I’ve got a house that was built in 1976, it was owned by my parents … uhm, we’re celebrating our 50, our 50-year anniversary on the house and that’s about to go if this goes ahead. Well, that’s if, if they decide to go on grade, I mean, this is literally cutting Sharonlea in half, if they chose to go in this exact line …

(Govan) The Gautrain launched in 2010, running between OR Tambo International Airport and Sandton, just in time for the FIFA World Cup. The new plans envisage an expansion from Mamelodi in the norther to Jabulani in Soweto in the south, and from Boksburg in the east, the Lanseria Airport in the west. Phase One is a thirty-two kilometre connection between the existing Marlboro Station near Sandton to a new station here in Little Falls – a route with a direct impact on Sharonlea. Residents here were told that a proposed route will follow one of three options through the suburb.

(Govan) JC says options were presented to residents but that nothing is decided as yet …

(JC Wouters) So, these are the three lines. The red line is the PWV 3 which is what we preferred as you can see it runs through the road reserves – minimal impact on houses – the blue line runs further south and then the green line is what they ended up going for … the green line’s got a viaduct which is what is crossing over Sharon Valley and then it tunnels at the school and then continues through – I mean you can see – it goes right through the area – through complexes.
(Govan): And is this firm decision or might this change
(JC Wouters) They said it’s not; they said that the line and the corridor could even shift but this is the information we’ve got … so because it can shift it can potentially be worse than what we’re seeing here we don’t know …

(Govan) JC believes his fellow residents understand that the Gautrain extensions are meant to connect cities for work and shopping but, says, only station areas will benefit, while others won’t.

(Govan) So, you’re doing the work but not getting the stations ...
(JC Wouters) Well, we’re not getting the benefits, that’s the thing … we’re expected to pay out of our tax paying money towards this – the rail – for the Patronage Guarantee and over and above that we’re expected to sell up our homes and give that up as well to Gautrain. We’re giving, giving, giving, and we don’t get the benefit of the rail, or the usage of it …

(Govan) Although no stations will be built in Sharonlea, tracks on the ground, and those overhead – known as viaducts – may become part of the landscape. University Professor and Sharonlea resident Edwin Mmutlane says while plans show he might not have a track running through his backyard, others won’t be spared.

(Edwin Mmutlane) I dread the idea of me having to live next to a railway line – even much worse if it is going to run above my roof, if it is the viaducts that they are going to construct. If it is underground, well the vibrations will be there, but maybe because the landscape won’t be that much altered I just want to survive until one is ready to sell and go buy someplace else.

(Govan) Houses, businesses, Sharonlea Primary School, and even areas around a local shopping centre and retirement village could be directly in the new train’s path. But there’s still confusion around what exactly to expect

(Govan) So where we’re standing currently that would be what, a pillar?
(Nicolette Joubert) That’s what we’re understanding but we … as far as we know there no real exact, there’s no real line yet … so that’s still being given to a contractor who will determine the line, so it could be here, but it could also be on the other side of this wall or on the other side of that wall. The problem is that if, I mean, they take this house that’s fine and we, and we are compensated for that, that’s fine but what if that viaduct is there, then my house is under the viaduct, know what I mean
(Govan) And you don’t get compensated for that
(Nicolette) And we get no compensation for that so that is a huge problem …
(Govan) What will you do?
(Nicolette) If the … if it was there? Well, the problem is you can’t even sell your house, who you going to sell it to?

(Govan) For now, the issue of who gets compensated and for what if tracks run through or even next to properties remains murky. The GMA has reportedly told residents this issue will be discussed later. But despite the uncertainty around costs, social impact, and the effect on neighbourhoods, Premier Lesufi is determined to forge ahead, saying the pay-off will be the creation of a hundred and twenty-five thousand jobs, and significant economic investment and development …

(Govan) We requested an interview with the Premier of Gauteng and his MEC of Transport about the Gautrain’s extensions. They declined to speak to us, instead they referred us to the Gautrain Management Agency …

(Govan) The reason why the Gautrain needs to expand is because …?
(Tshepo Kgobe) It’s because we have to be able to enable the economy of this province to grow and therefore we have to be able to bring people directly from points where they are residing into nodes that they want to go into.

(Govan) That was one of the main arguments put forward when the original Gautrain idea was first mooted in the early two thousands. So while comparisons aren’t always helpful, the current Gautrain service should shed some light on the wisdom of the planned extensions. For example, has the Gautrain delivered on its promises?

(Tshepo Kgobe) It has delivered on jobs, it has delivered on what do they call it, on reducing the congestion that was there originally …
(Govan) But it hasn’t reduced the congestion …
(Tshepo Kgobe) No, but let’s go back to it, you need to be able understand … when you argue it hasn’t reduced the congestion …
(Govan) No, you said the congestion is up to pre-Covid levels and has surpassed what it was before Covid, you said that …
(Tshepo Kgobe) We’re going back to that conversation. I’m giving you facts and then you then what do they call it, want to give it to me as this is I what I said…

(Govan) When pushed on the issue of congestion Kgobe referred to a 2019 report called “The Economic and Social Impact of Gautrain”. But, nowhere in this document – prepared by the GMA itself – is any data provided to support the claim that congestion on the freeway between Pretoria and Joburg has eased. In 2016 the GMA submitted a feasibility study to National Treasury motivating for the extensions. A decade on and the extension project is seemingly stuck in the station. But Kgobe believes Treasury’s approval is imminent – putting the extensions plans back on track…

(Tshepo Kgobe) We are at a point where they – what do they call it – the Treasury Approval One is about to be approved – we just need to update the modelling …
(Govan) It’s about to be approved?
(Tshepo Kgobe) Based on the updated numbers of the modelling, and everything else that we add to it and reworking the revenue model, because that becomes important…

(Govan) For the people of Sharonlea, news that Treasury approval for the next phase of planning is imminent will accelerate their anxiety about the project. They’ve submitted their objections and given their input, and all they can do for now is wait and see how the provincial government and the Gautrain Management Agency plans to develop their beloved neighbourhood…

If it is underground, well the vibrations will be there, but maybe because the landscape won’t be that much altered I just want to survive until one is ready to sell and go buy someplace else. (Govan) Houses, businesses, Sharonlea Primary School, and even areas around a local shopping centre and retirement village could be directly in the new train’s path. But there’s still confusion around what exactly to expect (Govan) So where we’re standing currently that would be what, a pillar? (Nicolette Joubert) That’s what we’re understanding but we … as far as we know there no real exact, there’s no real line yet … so that’s still being given to a contractor who will determine the line, so it could be here, but it could also be on the other side of this wall or on the other side of that wall. The problem is that if, I mean, they take this house that’s fine and we, and we are compensated for that, that’s fine but what if that viaduct is there, then my house is under the viaduct, know what I mean (Govan) And you don’t get compensated for that (Nicolette) And we get no compensation for that so that is a huge problem … (Govan) What will you do? (Nicolette) If the … if it was there? Well, the problem is you can’t even sell your house, who you going to sell it to? (Govan) For now, the issue of who gets compensated and for what if tracks run through or even next to properties remains murky. The GMA has reportedly told residents this issue will be discussed later. But despite the uncertainty around costs, social impact, and the effect on neighbourhoods, Premier Lesufi is determined to forge ahead, saying the pay-off will be the creation of a hundred and twenty-five thousand jobs, and significant economic investment and development … (Govan) We requested an interview with the Premier of Gauteng and his MEC of Transport about the Gautrain’s extensions. They declined to speak to us, instead they referred us to the Gautrain Management Agency … (Govan) The reason why the Gautrain needs to expand is because …? (Tshepo Kgobe) It’s because we have to be able to enable the economy of this province to grow and therefore we have to be able to bring people directly from points where they are residing into nodes that they want to go into. (Govan) That was one of the main arguments put forward when the original Gautrain idea was first mooted in the early two thousands. So while comparisons aren’t always helpful, the current Gautrain service should shed some light on the wisdom of the planned extensions. For example, has the Gautrain delivered on its promises? (Tshepo Kgobe) It has delivered on jobs, it has delivered on what do they call it, on reducing the congestion that was there originally … (Govan) But it hasn’t reduced the congestion … (Tshepo Kgobe) No, but let’s go back to it, you need to be able understand … when you argue it hasn’t reduced the congestion … (Govan) No, you said the congestion is up to pre-Covid levels and has surpassed what it was before Covid, you said that … (Tshepo Kgobe) We’re going back to that conversation. I’m giving you facts and then you then what do they call it, want to give it to me as this is I what I said… (Govan) When pushed on the issue of congestion Kgobe referred to a 2019 report called “The Economic and Social Impact of Gautrain”. But, nowhere in this document – prepared by the GMA itself – is any data provided to support the claim that congestion on the freeway between Pretoria and Joburg has eased. In 2016 the GMA submitted a feasibility study to National Treasury motivating for the extensions. A decade on and the extension project is seemingly stuck in the station. But Kgobe believes Treasury’s approval is imminent – putting the extensions plans back on track… (Tshepo Kgobe) We are at a point where they – what do they call it – the Treasury Approval One is about to be approved – we just need to update the modelling … (Govan) It’s about to be approved? (Tshepo Kgobe) Based on the updated numbers of the modelling, and everything else that we add to it and reworking the revenue model, because that becomes important… (Govan) For the people of Sharonlea, news that Treasury approval for the next phase of planning is imminent will accelerate their anxiety about the project. They’ve submitted their objections and given their input, and all they can do for now is wait and see how the provincial government and the Gautrain Management Agency plans to develop their beloved neighbourhood…

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight on Carte Blanche we ask if the proposed Gautrain expansion will transform the province’s transport, or be a fast-track to spending billions on a single project
metadata.Unique Selling Point: A comprehensive, easy-to-understand explanation of the current Gautrain costs, the proposed expansion plans, and what the people who are most affected have to say about it. Unlike other reports which have already been written on the proposed extensions, this story will unpack the contentious issue of the justification of the expansions, especially in the context of the current system which has already cost Gauteng taxpayers close to R23bn because of low ridership numbers.
metadata.Summary: Hailed as an answer to Gauteng’s congestion problems – specifically on the N1 between Tshwane and Johannesburg - the Gautrain has failed to reach pre-launch ridership numbers or reduce congestion. While it is world class, clean, on time, and safe, the Gautrain is also expensive and out of reach of poorer commuters, it is aimed at people who are already mobile, and it is running at a massive loss, costing taxpayers billions of Rands through the PG annually. Gautrain expenditure is also diverting funds from other transport solutions in poorer communities, raising the question of where the GPG’s priorities lie in providing mobility solutions for all in the province. In this context, is an extension of the service (which will cost additional billions to construct and maintain) viable and necessary, and why does the Gauteng Premier, his government, and the GMA believe it is? Critically, the piece will also ask the question of why there is so much secrecy around the project, and why the GPG and the GMA have been more forthcoming with the public.
metadata.Further information: Interviews with affected residents from Sharonlea and with the CEO of the Gautrain Management Agency - Tshepo Kgobe
